body:
What are the Vedas?

The Vedas are the oldest surviving collections of sacred literature in Sanskrit and among the earliest literary traditions of the Indian subcontinent. They contain hymns, prayers, ritual formulas, chants and reflections on human life and the natural world. They are also important historical sources because they provide information about the beliefs, occupations, communities and geographical surroundings of the people who composed them.

The word Veda comes from the Sanskrit root vid, meaning to know. Veda therefore means knowledge. In the Vedic religious tradition, this knowledge is regarded as sacred.

There are 4 Vedas:

  • Rigveda: A collection of hymns praising various deities.
  • Samaveda: A collection of chants arranged for melodic singing, largely using verses from the Rigveda.
  • Yajurveda: A collection of formulas and prayers used in performing sacrifices.
  • Atharvaveda: A collection of hymns, prayers and incantations concerning protection, healing, well-being and other aspects of life.

Each Veda has its own distinctive emphasis, although their contents overlap. For example, a verse originally preserved in the Rigveda may also appear in the Samaveda with a musical arrangement. The 4 Vedas should therefore be understood as related collections rather than completely separate subjects.

Why the Vedas are important for history

The Vedas were composed over a long period by different composers and communities. The oldest surviving Vedic collection is the Rigveda. Its hymns provide particularly valuable information about the early Vedic period, while the other Vedas and related literature help explain developments during the later Vedic period.

The Vedas are primarily religious and ritual texts, not chronological records written by historians. Nevertheless, references to cattle, agriculture, rivers, chiefs, assemblies and rituals help establish the basic features of the society in which their hymns developed.

For example, repeated Rigvedic prayers for cattle reveal the importance of cattle in economic life. References to rivers help identify the broad geographical setting of the early Vedic communities. Such references are historical evidence, although they do not describe every community living in the subcontinent.

The Vedas were originally an oral tradition

The Vedic hymns were initially composed, recited, memorised and transmitted orally. Teachers instructed students in the correct pronunciation, sequence and recitation of words. This transmission continued across generations before the texts were preserved in manuscripts.

The language of the earliest hymns was Vedic Sanskrit, an older form of Sanskrit that differs in important respects from later Classical Sanskrit.

Composition is not the same as writing

The approximate date assigned to a Vedic hymn concerns its composition, not the date of its oldest surviving manuscript. The Vedas existed as an oral tradition long before the surviving written copies were produced.

Basic chronological setting

A widely used textbook chronology divides the Vedic Age into 2 broad phases:

  • Early Vedic or Rigvedic period: approximately 1500–1000 BCE. The Rigveda is the principal literary source for this phase.
  • Later Vedic period: approximately 1000–600 BCE. The other Vedas and associated Vedic literature provide important evidence for developments during this phase.

These dates are approximate historical conventions rather than exact years when composition began or ended. Vedic texts developed across generations, and some literary traditions overlapped.

The distinction between early and later Vedic periods is based on changes in the geographical focus, economy, social organisation and literature of the communities described in the texts.

Prelims focus

  • The word Veda is derived from vid, meaning to know.
  • There are 4 Vedas: Rigveda, Samaveda, Yajurveda and Atharvaveda.
  • The Rigveda is the oldest surviving Vedic collection.
  • The original language of the Vedic hymns is Vedic Sanskrit.
  • Vedic literature was initially transmitted orally.
  • Trap: The date of a surviving manuscript is not the date when its hymns were originally composed.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 5, What Books and Burials Tell Us, printed pp. 43–44; NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, Chapter 7, India's Cultural Roots, printed pp. 106–107; National Institute of Open Schooling, Senior Secondary History, Lesson 4, The Vedic Age, printed pp. 48–49, consulted online on 17 November 2026.]

title: Understanding the Vedas: Meaning, Origin and Historical Importance

body:
Why the 4 Vedas have different contents

The 4 Vedas preserve related traditions of hymns, chants, prayers and rituals. Their distinguishing features are especially important when identifying which Veda contains a particular type of composition.

The simplest distinction is between hymns of praise, musical chanting, sacrificial formulas and prayers concerning everyday life. These categories describe the principal emphasis of each Veda rather than excluding all other kinds of content.

Rigveda: Hymns of praise

The Rigveda is the oldest of the 4 Vedas. It consists primarily of hymns addressed to various deities, including Agni, Indra and Soma.

These hymns express prayers for cattle, prosperity, protection, health, children and success. They also refer to rivers, occupations, warfare and social relationships, making the Rigveda a fundamental source for early Vedic history.

A Rigvedic hymn is called a sukta, meaning a well-spoken composition. The hymns were intended for recitation and were used in sacrificial worship.

Samaveda: Melodic chanting

The Samaveda is distinguished by the musical arrangement of sacred verses. Most of its verses are derived from the Rigveda and are adapted for singing during rituals, particularly Soma sacrifices.

Its importance lies in the manner of performance. A Rigvedic verse that is ordinarily recited may be arranged with a prescribed melody in the Samavedic tradition.

The Samaveda is therefore closely associated with the early tradition of Vedic music and chanting.

Rigveda versus Samaveda: The Rigveda primarily preserves hymns of praise; the Samaveda is especially concerned with their melodic performance. A verse can occur in both collections.

Yajurveda: Formulas for sacrificial rituals

The Yajurveda contains prayers and sacrificial formulas used by priests while performing ritual actions. Its mantras are arranged according to the requirements of particular sacrifices.

Unlike the Rigveda, which mainly preserves hymns of praise, the Yajurveda is particularly concerned with what is recited during the performance of a ritual. It includes material in both verse and prose.

The Yajurveda has 2 major textual traditions:

  • Shukla Yajurveda: Also called the White Yajurveda. Its Samhita presents sacrificial formulas separately from the associated explanatory Brahmana material.
  • Krishna Yajurveda: Also called the Black Yajurveda. Its Samhita contains sacrificial formulas interspersed with explanatory prose.

These names identify textual traditions, not separate Vedas or different historical periods.

Atharvaveda: Protection, healing and daily concerns

The Atharvaveda contains hymns, prayers and incantations connected with protection, recovery from illness, welfare, long life and other concerns of ordinary life.

Some compositions seek protection against misfortune or harmful influences, while others concern health, prosperity, family life and religious observances.

The Atharvaveda is consequently an important source for understanding popular beliefs and everyday concerns alongside formal Vedic religious traditions.

It is incorrect to treat the Atharvaveda as only a medical text or only a collection of magical spells. Its contents are broader and include devotional and speculative hymns.

How the 4 Vedas relate to ritual practice

During an elaborate Vedic sacrifice, sacred words could serve different purposes. Some hymns invoked deities, some were sung in prescribed melodies, and others accompanied specific ritual actions. The Atharvaveda also preserved prayers and formulas for protection and well-being, extending beyond the principal functions of the other collections.

The first 3 Vedas—Rigveda, Samaveda and Yajurveda—are sometimes collectively called the Veda-trayi, or Vedic triad. This traditional grouping does not mean that only 3 Vedas exist. The recognised collection contains 4 Vedas, including the Atharvaveda.

Prelims focus

  • Rigveda: Hymns praising deities; oldest Vedic collection.
  • Samaveda: Melodic chants, mostly adapted from Rigvedic verses.
  • Yajurveda: Sacrificial formulas and ritual recitations.
  • Atharvaveda: Prayers and incantations associated with protection, healing and everyday concerns.
  • Shukla and Krishna are the 2 major Yajurvedic traditions.
  • Trap: The Veda-trayi consists of 3 named Vedas, but the full Vedic collection contains 4.

[Sources: National Institute of Open Schooling, Senior Secondary History, Lesson 4, The Vedic Age, printed pp. 48–49; Indira Gandhi National Open University, MHI-06, Evolution of Social Structures in India Through the Ages, Block 2, Unit 4, Societies Represented in Vedic Literature, printed pp. 5–6; Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts, A Glimpse of Vedic Literature, section The Vedas, consulted online on 17 November 2026; UNESCO, Tradition of Vedic Chanting, Representative List entry 00062, consulted on 17 November 2026.]

title: The Four Vedas: Their Contents, Functions and Key Differences

body:
The structure of the Rigveda

The Rigveda is the principal literary source for understanding the early Vedic period. It is a collection of hymns composed in Vedic Sanskrit over several generations.

The commonly used count of the Rigveda is 1,028 hymns arranged in 10 mandalas, or books. Different textual counting conventions can produce small variations in the hymn total, but 1,028 is the standard figure used in many introductory history textbooks.

A mandala is a major division of the Rigveda, while a sukta is an individual hymn. Each hymn normally contains several verses, known as richas.

Mandalas 2–7 are commonly called the family books because they are associated with particular families or lineages of Vedic composers. They contain some of the earliest portions of the collection.

Who composed the hymns?

The hymns were composed by rishis, or sages and poet-seers. The Vedic tradition also preserves compositions associated with women, called rishikas.

Most hymns were composed, taught and transmitted within male-dominated priestly traditions, but the presence of women composers is an important qualification. It would be inaccurate to state that every Rigvedic hymn was composed by a man.

Because the Rigveda developed across generations, it should not be attributed to a single author.

Important Rigvedic deities

Many Rigvedic hymns praise deities associated with natural forces, protection, prosperity and the maintenance of order.

DeityPrincipal associationHistorical significance
AgniFire and sacrificial fireOfferings were made through fire during rituals.
IndraWar, strength, storms and rainFrequently invoked for victory and protection.
SomaSacred plant and ritual drinkAssociated with an important Vedic sacrificial offering.
VarunaCosmic and moral orderAssociated with the maintenance of rita.
UshasDawnPraised in hymns celebrating the arrival of morning.

Rita refers to the order or regularity governing the natural and moral world. Varuna is particularly associated with its preservation in Vedic religious thought.

These associations identify prominent themes, but the characteristics of Vedic deities can overlap across different hymns.

What Rigvedic prayers reveal about society

The hymns frequently ask for cattle, horses, children, prosperity, victory and long life. These requests show what many composers and their communities valued.

Cattle were economically important, while horses and chariots were associated with transport and warfare. Hymns also refer to conflicts over cattle, land and water.

However, a hymn is a religious or poetic composition. A prayer for a large herd does not prove that every household possessed many cattle. Such references reveal social priorities more directly than they reveal the exact distribution of wealth.

Rivers and the geographical setting

The Rigveda contains references to several rivers of northwestern South Asia, especially the Indus and its tributaries.

A well-known dialogue hymn presents the sage Vishvamitra addressing the rivers Beas and Sutlej. The rivers are represented as speaking beings, and the dialogue concerns the safe crossing of their waters.

The geographical references help connect the composition with the northwestern river region. References to cattle, horses, chariots and carts also provide information about the material environment familiar to the composers.

The Rigveda mentions rivers such as the Sindhu and Sarasvati, whereas the Ganga and Yamuna receive comparatively limited attention. This is consistent with the mainly northwestern geographical focus of the oldest Vedic collection.

The Rigveda is simultaneously a religious text and a historical source. Its hymns provide evidence about beliefs and social life, but poetic descriptions should not automatically be treated as literal accounts of events.

Prelims focus

  • The Rigveda contains approximately 1,028 hymns arranged in 10 mandalas.
  • A mandala is a book or major division; a sukta is a hymn.
  • Mandalas 2–7 are commonly known as the family books.
  • Agni, Indra and Soma are especially prominent Rigvedic deities.
  • The dialogue involving Vishvamitra, Beas and Sutlej occurs in the Rigveda.
  • Trap: The Rigveda was not composed by one author, and not every hymn was composed by a man.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 5, What Books and Burials Tell Us, printed pp. 43–47; National Institute of Open Schooling, Senior Secondary History, Lesson 4, The Vedic Age, printed pp. 49 and 56–57; Indira Gandhi National Open University, MHI-06, Block 2, Unit 4, Societies Represented in Vedic Literature, printed pp. 5–6; NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, Chapter 7, India's Cultural Roots, printed pp. 106–108.]
